extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103, including how modifications (making portable/integral/separable/adjustable/continuous), range overlaps, routine optimization, equivalence, and genus-to-species issues affect prima facie obviousness and rebuttal. Intended to direct examination and the showing required by examiners and applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making Portable
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact that a claimed device is portable or movable is not sufficient by itself to patentably distinguish over an otherwise old device unless there are new or unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: In re Lindberg, 194 F.2d 732, 93 USPQ 23 (CCPA 1952). Portability alone is not a patentable distinction; applicant must show new or unexpected results from making the device portable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making Integral
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a one-piece (integral) construction instead of multiple parts is often merely an obvious engineering choice unless the one-piece construction produces insight or results contrary to the understandings and expectations of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: In re Larson (integral brake drum held obvious as matter of design choice); contrast Schenck v. Nortron Corp., 713 F.2d 782, 218 USPQ 698 (Fed. Cir. 1983) where a one-piece gapless support structure eliminated the need for dampening and was found patentable because it showed insight contrary to the art. Examiner should evaluate whether the integral construction yields new/unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making Separable
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting a non-removable part into a removable/separable part is obvious if it would have been an obvious modification to obtain access or functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: In re Dulberg, 289 F.2d 522, 129 USPQ 348 (CCPA 1961). If access or another motivation exists in the prior art, making a cap removable (or otherwise separable) is an obvious change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making Adjustable
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing adjustability where the art recognizes a need for adjustment is not a patentable advance; substitution of known mechanisms to achieve adjustment may be obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: In re Stevens, 212 F.2d 197, 101 USPQ 284 (CCPA 1954) (adjustable fishing rod handle using a universal joint was held obvious). Examiner should consider whether adjustment was art-recognized and whether substitution is routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making Continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting a batch process to continuous operation is obvious when the claimed continuous operation would have been an obvious modification of the prior batch process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: In re Dilnot, 319 F.2d 188, 138 USPQ 248 (CCPA 1963). If prior art teaches batch processing, continuous addition/operation may be routine engineering optimization absent unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely reversing movement or arrangement of parts (reversal of parts) is an obvious modification when it does not change the operation in any meaningful way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: In re Gazda (clock movement reversal held obvious). Examiner should determine whether reversal modifies operation or produces new/unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication of Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere duplication of parts has no patentable significance unless the duplication produces a new and unexpected result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: In re Harza, 274 F.2d 669, 124 USPQ 378 (CCPA 1960). If duplication yields no novel function or unexpected property, it is not a basis for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rearrangement of Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Repositioning or rearranging parts is obvious where the change does not modify the device's operation and is a matter of design choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: In re Japikse, 181 F.2d 1019, 86 USPQ 70 (CCPA 1950); In re Kuhle, 526 F.2d 553, 188 USPQ 7 (CCPA 1975). Examiner should ask whether placement changes alter operation or yield unexpected benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purifying an Old Product
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to purified forms of known products are evaluated for obviousness by considering whether the claimed compound/composition has the same utility as prior art, whether prior art suggests the particular form or structure, or methods to obtain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include whether the purified material has structural/functional differences and whether prior art suggests the form or means to obtain it. Case: In re Cofer (crystalline form held nonobvious where prior art didn't suggest crystalline form or how to obtain it). Improvement in process increasing purity does not render product patentable if purified product has no structural/functional difference (see Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma). See MPEP § 2113 and Ex parte Stern for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping, Approaching, and Similar Ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: When claimed ranges overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art, a prima facie case of obviousness exists; ranges that are merely close (approaching) can also support a prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: In re Wertheim; In re Woodruff; In re Geisler; In re Bergen. Overlapping endpoints can be sufficient, and non-overlapping but close numerical differences may be insufficient to show patentability absent criticality or unexpected results (see Titanium Metals Corp. of America v. Banner; In re Aller; In re Becket; In re Dreyfus). A single claimed value within a prior art 'range' disclosed across multiple references can still be presumed obvious (Iron Grip Barbell Co. v. USA Sports). Consider whether prior art range is so broad as to be analogous to a genus (see In re Baird). See also MPEP § 2144.08 for broad range discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine Optimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovering optimum or workable ranges within conditions disclosed in the prior art by routine experimentation is typically obvious unless evidence indicates the concentration/temperature/parameter is critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: In re Aller; In re Hoeschele; Merck & Co. v. Biocraft; In re Kulling; In re Geisler. The 'normal desire' to improve known art provides motivation to determine optimum percentages. Smith v. Nichols, In re Williams cited. Examiner should require evidence of criticality or unexpected results to overcome routine optimization. See KSR for caution in combining known elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulated Rationale Required for Routine Optimization Rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: To properly support a rejection based on routine optimization, the examiner must make factual findings and present the underpinning reasoning, explaining why it would have been routine to arrive at the claimed invention and why a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: In re Stepan; In re Van Os; Arendi S.A.R.L. v. Apple. After KSR, 'obvious to try' can be a valid rationale when there is a design need/market demand and a finite number of predictable solutions. References to 'common sense' cannot substitute for reasoned analysis without articulated rationale and evidentiary support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal — Showing That the Range Is Critical
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness by showing that the claimed range is critical, normally by showing the claimed range achieves unexpected results relative to the prior art range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden on applicant to establish facts showing criticality. Cases: In re Woodruff; Minerals Separation v. Hyde; In re Scherl; In re Becket; E.I. DuPont de Nemours & Co. v. Synvina C.V.; In re Lilienfeld. Evidence should show a difference in kind (new property) rather than merely a difference in degree. See MPEP § 716.02–§ 716.02(g) for criticality and unexpected results discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal — Showing That the Prior Art Teaches Away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness may be rebutted by showing that the prior art, in any material respect, teaches away from the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: U.S. v. Adams; Depuy Spine v. Medtronic; Allergan v. Sandoz. Teaching away is especially strong where prior art undermines the reason for combining elements. Demonstrating teaching away requires showing the prior art would have discouraged one of ordinary skill from the claimed approach (see In re Geisler for discussion of when a reference does not teach away). See MPEP § 2145 X.D. for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal — Showing That the Claimed Parameter Was Not Recognized as Result-Effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may rebut obviousness by showing the claimed variable was not recognized in the prior art to be a result-effective variable, making optimization of that variable an exception to routine optimization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle from Antonie: if prior art is silent on the variable's effect on the result, optimization may be nonobvious. Cases: E.I. Dupont v. Synvina; In re Antonie; Applied Materials discussion. Applicant must articulate why the variable would not have been seen in the prior art as result-effective. Note that after KSR, recognition of a result-effective variable is one, but not the only, motivation for experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal — Very Broad Prior Art Range May Weigh Against Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art discloses a very broad range that encompasses members with dissimilar characteristics, that disclosure may not invite optimization and can weigh against maintaining an obviousness rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Genetics Inst. v. Novartis (disclosure of 68,000 protein variants where claimed truncated proteins vary enormously in structure). See MPEP §§ 2131.02, 2131.03, and 2144.08 for additional discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining Equivalents Known for the Same Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: It is prima facie obvious to combine two compositions each of which is taught by the prior art to be useful for the same purpose, in order to form a third composition to be used for the very same purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: In re Kerkhoven (mixing two conventional spray-dried detergents held prima facie obvious). Other examples include mixtures of known herbicides (Ex parte Quadranti) and materials where components individually promote the same effect (In re Crockett). Examiner should consider whether the prior art teaches each component's utility for the purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substituting Equivalents Known for the Same Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting one equivalent component for another known to serve the same purpose can support an obviousness rejection when the equivalency is recognized in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: In re Ruff; Smith v. Hayashi. The equivalency must be recognized in the prior art (not merely an applicant's Markush listing or applicant's disclosure). An express suggestion to substitute is not necessary to render substitution obvious (In re Fout). Examiner should look for art-recognized equivalence evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art Recognized Suitability for an Intended Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of a known material based on its suitability for an intended use supports a prima facie obviousness determination if prior art recognizes the material's suitability for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Sinclair & Carroll Co. v. Interchemical (selection of a solvent with specific vapor pressure characteristics held invalid). Example: selection of a known plastic for a container or replacing mechanical with hydraulic brakes where hydraulics were known to do same function (Ryco, Inc. v. Ag-Bag Corp.). Equivalence must be recognized in prior art and cannot be based solely on applicant's disclosure or mere functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness of Species When Prior Art Teaches Genus — Examination Guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When a single prior art reference discloses a genus encompassing the claimed species but not the particular species, Office personnel should search for additional prior art and, if none is found, evaluate factors to determine whether a single-reference 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office should attempt to find additional prior art to show that the differences between the primary reference and the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious. If additional prior art is not found, consider whether the claimed species or subgenus would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill at the relevant time (see further subsections for factors). This guidance applies regardless of AIA or pre-AIA timing rules (see header note).
